meta.subject: english
meta.description: Grammar facts: parts of speech, punctuation rules, sentence types, subject-verb agreement, verb tenses, pronouns, clauses

facts.statement: There are eight parts of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, interjection
A noun names a person, place, thing, or idea
A verb expresses an action or state of being
An adjective modifies (describes) a noun or pronoun
An adverb modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb, often ending in -ly
A preposition shows the relationship between a noun/pronoun and another word (in, on, at, by, for, with, about, between)
A conjunction connects words, phrases, or clauses (and, but, or, so, yet, for, nor)
An interjection expresses emotion and is often followed by an exclamation point (wow!, ouch!, hey!)
A pronoun takes the place of a noun (he, she, it, they, we, us, them, who, which)
A common noun is a general name (city, dog), while a proper noun names a specific person, place, or thing (Chicago, Rover) and is always capitalized
An abstract noun names an idea, quality, or state that cannot be physically touched (freedom, happiness, justice, love)
A collective noun names a group (team, flock, audience, committee)
Articles (a, an, the) are a type of adjective; 'a' and 'an' are indefinite articles, 'the' is the definite article
Use 'an' before words that begin with a vowel sound (an apple, an hour) and 'a' before consonant sounds (a dog, a university)
Coordinating conjunctions (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) join equal grammatical elements
Subordinating conjunctions (because, although, while, if, when, since, until) begin dependent clauses

common_errors.wrong: adverbs only modify verbs
common_errors.correct: Adverbs can modify verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs. 'She ran very quickly' - 'very' modifies the adverb 'quickly.'

common_errors.wrong: all adverbs end in -ly
common_errors.correct: Many adverbs do not end in -ly: 'fast', 'well', 'never', 'always', 'very', 'here', 'there', 'soon', 'often.'

common_errors.wrong: a word can only be one part of speech
common_errors.correct: Many words can function as different parts of speech depending on context. 'Run' can be a verb ('I run') or a noun ('a good run').

common_errors.wrong: use 'a' before all words starting with vowel letters
common_errors.correct: Use 'an' based on the SOUND, not the letter. 'An hour' (silent h) but 'a university' (starts with 'yoo' sound).

common_errors.wrong: proper nouns are always people's names
common_errors.correct: Proper nouns include specific places (Paris), organizations (NASA), days (Monday), months (January), holidays, and brand names.

facts.statement: A period ends a declarative or imperative sentence
A comma separates items in a list, joins independent clauses with a conjunction, and sets off introductory elements
A semicolon joins two related independent clauses without a conjunction
A colon introduces a list, explanation, or elaboration that follows an independent clause
An apostrophe shows possession (dog's bone) or marks contractions (don't, isn't)
Quotation marks enclose direct speech or titles of short works like poems, short stories, and articles
The Oxford (serial) comma is the comma before 'and' in a list of three or more items, and its use is a matter of style
A hyphen joins compound adjectives before a noun (well-known author), while an em dash sets off parenthetical information
A comma splice is the error of joining two independent clauses with only a comma (no conjunction); it can be fixed with a period, semicolon, or adding a conjunction
A run-on sentence occurs when two independent clauses are joined without proper punctuation or a conjunction
In American English, periods and commas go inside quotation marks; semicolons and colons go outside
An ellipsis (...) indicates omitted words in a quotation or a trailing off in speech
For singular possessives, add 's (the cat's toy); for plural possessives ending in s, add only an apostrophe (the dogs' park)
Parentheses enclose supplementary information that could be removed without changing the sentence's meaning
Use a comma after introductory words, phrases, or clauses: 'However, I disagree.' 'After dinner, we left.'

common_errors.wrong: its and it's mean the same thing
common_errors.correct: 'Its' (no apostrophe) is possessive: 'The dog wagged its tail.' 'It's' is a contraction of 'it is' or 'it has.'

common_errors.wrong: you always put a comma before 'and'
common_errors.correct: A comma before 'and' depends on context. Use one when joining independent clauses or in a serial list, but not when joining just two items.

common_errors.wrong: a semicolon works like a comma
common_errors.correct: A semicolon joins two independent clauses. A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice error.

common_errors.wrong: apostrophes make words plural
common_errors.correct: Apostrophes show possession or contractions, not plurals. 'Dogs' is plural; 'dog's' is possessive.

common_errors.wrong: you can use a comma to join any two sentences
common_errors.correct: Two independent clauses need more than a comma. Use a comma + conjunction, a semicolon, or a period. A comma alone creates a comma splice.

common_errors.wrong: a colon can follow any word
common_errors.correct: A colon must follow an independent clause. 'My favorites are: red, blue, green' is wrong; 'My favorites are red, blue, and green' or 'I have three favorites: red, blue, and green.'

facts.statement: A declarative sentence makes a statement and ends with a period
An interrogative sentence asks a question and ends with a question mark
An imperative sentence gives a command or request and often has an implied subject 'you'
An exclamatory sentence expresses strong emotion and ends with an exclamation point
A simple sentence contains one independent clause
A compound sentence contains two or more independent clauses joined by a conjunction or semicolon
A complex sentence contains one independent clause and one or more dependent clauses
A compound-complex sentence has at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause
An independent clause has a subject and predicate and can stand alone as a sentence
A dependent (subordinate) clause has a subject and predicate but cannot stand alone; it begins with a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun
A sentence fragment is an incomplete sentence that lacks a subject, a predicate, or does not express a complete thought
Every complete sentence must have a subject (who or what) and a predicate (what the subject does or is)
The subject of a sentence is who or what the sentence is about; the predicate contains the verb and tells what the subject does

common_errors.wrong: a long sentence is always a compound or complex sentence
common_errors.correct: Sentence classification depends on clause structure, not length. A long sentence with one subject-verb pair is still simple.

common_errors.wrong: imperative sentences always end with exclamation points
common_errors.correct: Imperative sentences can end with periods (Please sit down.) or exclamation points (Stop!) depending on the tone.

common_errors.wrong: a dependent clause can stand alone as a sentence
common_errors.correct: A dependent clause cannot stand alone; it needs an independent clause to form a complete sentence. Standing alone, it is a fragment.

common_errors.wrong: starting a sentence with 'because' always makes a fragment
common_errors.correct: 'Because' starts a dependent clause, which is fine if attached to an independent clause: 'Because it rained, we stayed inside.'

common_errors.wrong: a compound sentence must use 'and'
common_errors.correct: Compound sentences can use any coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) or a semicolon.

facts.statement: A singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb: 'The dog runs' (singular) vs. 'The dogs run' (plural)
Compound subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb: 'Tom and Jerry are friends'
Compound subjects joined by 'or' or 'nor' agree with the subject closest to the verb: 'Neither the cats nor the dog is outside'
Collective nouns (team, family, group) usually take a singular verb when acting as one unit: 'The team is winning'
Indefinite pronouns like 'everyone,' 'each,' 'nobody,' and 'anyone' take singular verbs: 'Everyone is here'
Indefinite pronouns like 'both,' 'few,' 'many,' and 'several' take plural verbs: 'Many are called'
Words between the subject and verb (prepositional phrases) do not affect agreement: 'The box of books is heavy' (box is singular)
In questions and sentences beginning with 'there' or 'here,' the subject follows the verb: 'There are many reasons'
The pronoun 'I' takes special verb forms: 'I am' (not 'I is'), 'I was' (not 'I were'), 'I have' (not 'I has')

common_errors.wrong: 'everyone' and 'everybody' take plural verbs because they refer to many people
common_errors.correct: 'Everyone' and 'everybody' are grammatically singular: 'Everyone is invited' (not 'Everyone are invited').

common_errors.wrong: 'the team are' is correct because there are multiple players
common_errors.correct: In American English, collective nouns like 'team' typically take a singular verb: 'The team is playing well.'

common_errors.wrong: the verb agrees with the closest noun
common_errors.correct: The verb agrees with the subject, not the nearest noun. 'The box of books IS heavy' (subject is 'box,' not 'books').

common_errors.wrong: 'there's' can be used with plural nouns
common_errors.correct: 'There's' means 'there is' (singular). For plurals, use 'there are': 'There are many options' (not 'There's many options').

facts.statement: The three main tenses are past, present, and future; each has simple, progressive, and perfect forms
Regular verbs form the past tense by adding -ed: walk/walked, play/played, talk/talked
Irregular verbs do not follow the -ed pattern: go/went, eat/ate, see/saw, run/ran, write/wrote, take/took
The present progressive tense uses 'am/is/are' + verb-ing to show ongoing action: 'She is running'
The past progressive tense uses 'was/were' + verb-ing to show ongoing past action: 'He was sleeping'
The present perfect tense uses 'has/have' + past participle: 'I have eaten' (action completed at an unspecified past time)
The past perfect tense uses 'had' + past participle: 'She had left before I arrived' (one past action before another)
The future tense uses 'will' + verb: 'They will arrive tomorrow'
Helping (auxiliary) verbs include: am, is, are, was, were, have, has, had, do, does, did, will, shall, would, could, should, may, might, must, can
A gerund is a verb form ending in -ing used as a noun: 'Swimming is fun' (swimming is the subject)
An infinitive is 'to' + base verb: 'to run,' 'to eat,' 'to learn.' It can function as a noun, adjective, or adverb
Common irregular past tenses: be/was-were, have/had, do/did, say/said, make/made, know/knew, think/thought, come/came, give/gave, find/found

common_errors.wrong: all past tenses are formed by adding -ed
common_errors.correct: Only regular verbs add -ed. Irregular verbs change form: go/went, eat/ate, swim/swam, bring/brought. Irregulars must be memorized.

common_errors.wrong: 'I seen' is correct past tense
common_errors.correct: 'Seen' is the past participle and needs a helping verb: 'I have seen' or 'I saw.' 'I seen' is nonstandard.

common_errors.wrong: 'I could of gone' is correct
common_errors.correct: The correct form is 'could have gone' (contracted: could've). 'Could of' is a common spelling error based on how 'could've' sounds.

common_errors.wrong: you can mix tenses freely in the same paragraph
common_errors.correct: Verb tenses should be consistent within a passage. Shift tenses only when the time frame actually changes.

common_errors.wrong: 'he don't' is correct grammar
common_errors.correct: The correct form is 'he doesn't' (does not). 'Don't' is used with I, you, we, they. 'Doesn't' is used with he, she, it.

facts.statement: Subject pronouns are used as the subject of a sentence: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
Object pronouns receive the action or follow a preposition: me, you, him, her, it, us, them
Possessive pronouns show ownership: my/mine, your/yours, his, her/hers, its, our/ours, their/theirs
A pronoun's antecedent is the noun it refers to; pronouns must agree in number and gender with their antecedent
'Who' is a subject pronoun (Who is calling?); 'whom' is an object pronoun (To whom did you speak?)
Reflexive pronouns reflect back to the subject: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, themselves
Relative pronouns (who, whom, whose, which, that) introduce relative clauses that modify nouns
Use 'I' as a subject and 'me' as an object. Test by removing the other person: 'She and I went' (I went), 'Give it to him and me' (give it to me)

common_errors.wrong: 'me and him went to the store' is correct
common_errors.correct: Subject pronouns are needed: 'He and I went to the store.' Test: 'I went' (not 'me went') and 'he went' (not 'him went').

common_errors.wrong: 'between you and I' is correct because 'I' sounds more formal
common_errors.correct: 'Between' is a preposition, so object pronouns follow: 'between you and me.' 'I' is never used after a preposition.

common_errors.wrong: 'everyone should bring their book' has incorrect agreement
common_errors.correct: While grammatically 'everyone' is singular, using 'their' as a singular pronoun is widely accepted: 'Everyone should bring their book.'

common_errors.wrong: 'whose' and 'who's' are the same
common_errors.correct: 'Whose' is possessive (Whose book is this?). 'Who's' is a contraction of 'who is' (Who's coming?).

facts.statement: A phrase is a group of related words that does not contain both a subject and a verb acting as a predicate
A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition and ends with a noun or pronoun (the object): 'in the park,' 'before noon'
An adjective clause (relative clause) modifies a noun and usually begins with who, whom, whose, which, or that
An adverb clause modifies a verb, adjective, or adverb and begins with a subordinating conjunction (because, when, although, if)
A noun clause functions as a noun in a sentence: 'What she said surprised everyone' (subject); 'I know that he is right' (object)
A participial phrase uses a present (-ing) or past (-ed/-en) participle to modify a noun: 'Running quickly, the dog caught the ball'
An appositive is a noun or phrase that renames or explains another noun right beside it: 'My brother, a doctor, lives in Boston'
A gerund phrase includes a gerund (-ing verb used as noun) and its modifiers: 'Playing chess requires patience'
An infinitive phrase includes an infinitive (to + verb) and its modifiers: 'To win the game was her only goal'
A restrictive (essential) clause is necessary to identify the noun and uses no commas: 'The student who studied passed'
A nonrestrictive (nonessential) clause adds extra information and is set off by commas: 'My sister, who lives in Texas, visited'

common_errors.wrong: all -ing words are gerunds
common_errors.correct: An -ing word is a gerund only when used as a noun. 'Swimming is fun' (gerund/noun). 'The swimming fish' (adjective/participle). 'She is swimming' (verb/progressive).

common_errors.wrong: a phrase and a clause are the same thing
common_errors.correct: A clause has a subject and a verb; a phrase does not. 'After dinner' is a phrase. 'After we ate dinner' is a clause.

common_errors.wrong: nonrestrictive clauses don't need commas
common_errors.correct: Nonrestrictive (nonessential) clauses MUST be set off by commas: 'My dog, who is very old, sleeps all day.' Without commas, it implies you have multiple dogs.

common_errors.wrong: you can dangle a participial phrase without consequence
common_errors.correct: A dangling modifier lacks a clear subject: 'Running to class, the bell rang' is wrong (the bell wasn't running). Fix: 'Running to class, I heard the bell ring.'

facts.statement: In active voice, the subject performs the action: 'The cat chased the mouse'
In passive voice, the subject receives the action: 'The mouse was chased by the cat'
Passive voice uses a form of 'be' (is, was, were, been) + past participle: 'The cake was eaten'
Active voice is generally preferred in writing because it is more direct and concise
Passive voice is appropriate when the actor is unknown, unimportant, or obvious: 'The window was broken' (unknown actor)
Scientific writing often uses passive voice: 'The solution was heated to 100 degrees'
Only transitive verbs (verbs that take a direct object) can be made passive; intransitive verbs like 'sleep' and 'arrive' cannot
The 'by phrase' in passive voice identifies the agent (doer): 'The book was written by the author'

common_errors.wrong: passive voice is always wrong
common_errors.correct: Passive voice is a valid grammatical construction. It's preferred when the actor is unknown, when focusing on the action/result, or in scientific writing.

common_errors.wrong: any sentence with 'was' is passive voice
common_errors.correct: 'Was' can be a linking verb (He was happy), past progressive (He was running), or passive (He was chased). Only 'was + past participle' with a received action is passive.

common_errors.wrong: 'The dog is sleeping' is passive because it uses 'is + -ing'
common_errors.correct: 'Is sleeping' is present progressive (active voice). Passive requires 'is + past participle': 'The dog is walked every morning.'

common_errors.wrong: passive voice always needs a 'by' phrase
common_errors.correct: The 'by' phrase is optional and often omitted: 'Mistakes were made' is passive without naming who made them.

facts.statement: Parallel structure means using the same grammatical form for items in a series: 'She likes reading, writing, and painting' (all gerunds)
Correlative conjunctions (either/or, neither/nor, not only/but also, both/and) require parallel structure on both sides
Comparisons should use parallel structure: 'She prefers swimming to running' (not 'swimming to run')
In lists, all items should be the same part of speech or structure: nouns with nouns, phrases with phrases, clauses with clauses
Faulty parallelism occurs when items in a series shift grammatical form: 'I like to swim, running, and play tennis' (mixes infinitive, gerund, and infinitive)
Parallel structure applies to headings, bullet points, and outlines in formal writing for clarity and consistency
With 'not only...but also,' both parts must have the same structure: 'She not only sings but also dances' (both verbs)

common_errors.wrong: mixing verb forms in a list is acceptable if the meaning is clear
common_errors.correct: Correct parallelism requires consistent form: 'I enjoy reading, writing, and painting' (all gerunds), not 'I enjoy reading, to write, and painting.'

common_errors.wrong: 'either you apologize or leaving' is correct
common_errors.correct: Correlative conjunctions need parallel forms: 'Either you apologize or you leave' (both clauses) or 'Either apologize or leave' (both imperatives).

common_errors.wrong: parallelism only matters in formal writing
common_errors.correct: Parallelism improves clarity in all writing. 'The dog ran, jumped, and was swimming' is awkward even in casual writing. Fix: 'ran, jumped, and swam.'

facts.statement: 'Their' is possessive (their house), 'there' indicates place (over there), 'they're' is a contraction of 'they are'
'Your' is possessive (your book), 'you're' is a contraction of 'you are' (you're welcome)
'To' is a preposition or infinitive marker, 'too' means 'also' or 'excessively,' 'two' is the number 2
'Affect' is usually a verb meaning to influence; 'effect' is usually a noun meaning the result: 'The rain affected the game. The effect was a delay.'
'Then' refers to time or sequence; 'than' is used for comparisons: 'First we ate, then we left. She is taller than her sister.'
'Accept' means to receive or agree; 'except' means to exclude: 'I accept the invitation. Everyone came except Maria.'
'Lose' is a verb meaning to misplace or fail to win; 'loose' is an adjective meaning not tight: 'Don't lose your keys. The knot is loose.'
'Weather' refers to atmospheric conditions; 'whether' introduces alternatives: 'Check the weather. I don't know whether to go.'
'Lie' means to recline (lie, lay, lain); 'lay' means to put down (lay, laid, laid): 'I lie on the bed. I lay the book on the table.'
'Farther' refers to physical distance; 'further' refers to degree or extent: 'We walked farther. Let's discuss this further.'
'Who' is a subject pronoun; 'whom' is an object pronoun. Test: replace with he/him. 'Who called?' (He called.) 'To whom?' (To him.)
'Less' is for uncountable nouns (less water); 'fewer' is for countable nouns (fewer cookies): 'Less noise. Fewer students.'
'Principal' is the head of a school or means 'main'; 'principle' is a rule or belief: 'The principal announced a new principle of conduct.'
'Stationary' means not moving; 'stationery' means writing materials: 'The car was stationary. She bought new stationery.'
'Complement' means to complete or enhance; 'compliment' means praise: 'The scarf complements her outfit. She received a compliment.'
'Emigrate' means to leave a country; 'immigrate' means to enter a country: 'She emigrated from Italy and immigrated to America.'
'Allude' means to hint at indirectly; 'elude' means to escape: 'The poem alludes to Greek mythology. The thief eluded capture.'
'Disinterested' means unbiased; 'uninterested' means not interested: 'A judge should be disinterested. The student was uninterested in math.'

common_errors.wrong: 'their,' 'there,' and 'they're' are interchangeable
common_errors.correct: Each has a specific meaning: 'their' = possessive (their car), 'there' = place (over there), 'they're' = they are (they're coming).

common_errors.wrong: 'affect' and 'effect' mean the same thing
common_errors.correct: 'Affect' is usually a verb (the cold affects my health); 'effect' is usually a noun (the effect of cold). Tip: Affect=Action, Effect=End result.

common_errors.wrong: 'less' and 'fewer' are interchangeable
common_errors.correct: 'Fewer' is for things you can count (fewer apples), 'less' is for things you can't count (less sugar). '10 items or fewer' is correct.

common_errors.wrong: 'i.e.' and 'e.g.' mean the same thing
common_errors.correct: 'i.e.' means 'that is' (clarifies), 'e.g.' means 'for example' (gives examples). 'She likes citrus, i.e., oranges and lemons' vs 'She likes fruit, e.g., apples and bananas.'

common_errors.wrong: 'literally' can mean 'figuratively'
common_errors.correct: While informal usage has blurred the line, in standard English 'literally' means 'actually/exactly as stated,' not as an intensifier for exaggeration.

common_errors.wrong: 'lay' and 'lie' are the same verb
common_errors.correct: 'Lie' (to recline) is intransitive: lie, lay, lain. 'Lay' (to put down) is transitive and needs an object: lay, laid, laid. 'I lie down' vs 'I lay the book down.'

common_errors.wrong: 'who' and 'whom' are interchangeable in all cases
common_errors.correct: Use 'who' as a subject (Who is there? = He is there) and 'whom' as an object (To whom? = To him). The he/him test works reliably.

common_errors.wrong: 'good' and 'well' are the same
common_errors.correct: 'Good' is an adjective (a good book); 'well' is usually an adverb (she writes well). Exception: 'I feel well' (healthy) vs 'I feel good' (happy).

facts.statement: Always capitalize the first word of a sentence, the pronoun 'I,' and proper nouns (specific names of people, places, organizations)
Capitalize days of the week (Monday), months (January), and holidays (Thanksgiving), but not seasons (spring, summer) unless part of a proper name

In titles, capitalize the first and last words and all major words; do not capitalize short prepositions (in, on, at), articles (a, an, the), or short conjunctions (and, but, or) unless they start the title
Capitalize geographic names (Pacific Ocean, Rocky Mountains), but not general geographic terms (the ocean, the mountains) unless part of a proper name
Capitalize titles when used before a name (President Lincoln, Dr. Smith) but not when used alone or after a name (the president, the doctor)

common_errors.wrong: seasons should be capitalized like months
common_errors.correct: Seasons (spring, summer, fall, winter) are NOT capitalized unless they begin a sentence or are part of a proper name (Spring Break, Winter Olympics).

common_errors.wrong: capitalize every word in a title
common_errors.correct: In title case, do NOT capitalize short prepositions (in, on, at, to), articles (a, an, the), or short conjunctions (and, but, or) unless they are the first or last word.

common_errors.wrong: always capitalize 'mom' and 'dad'
common_errors.correct: Capitalize family titles when used as proper names (I asked Mom) but not when preceded by a possessive (I asked my mom). Test: can you replace it with a name?
